items.title: OpenAI partners with Google Cloud to offer frontier models and Codex workflows through Google Cloud's Model Garden and Marketplace [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: OpenAI and Google Cloud have partnered to integrate OpenAI's frontier models and Codex agentic workflows into Google Cloud's Model Garden, enabling customers to access these models natively within Google Cloud's infrastructure. This integration supports complex AI workflows at scale while providing enterprises with data governance and access controls suited for regulated industries. The models will be available for purchase through the Google Cloud Marketplace, allowing enterprises with Google Cloud spend commitments to apply those credits. OpenAI models will also be accessible via Google Antigravity and the Gemini Agent, offering customers flexibility in model selection. General availability is planned in the coming weeks, expanding enterprise options for deploying frontier AI models within Google Cloud environments.

items.title: OpenAI leads global coalition to coordinate response and patch critical PHP vulnerabilities discovered by AI agents [ * ] [ ⬢ ]
items.content_text: OpenAI coordinated with PHP maintainers, security researchers, and providers to address critical vulnerabilities found in the PHP programming language using AI models like GPT-5.6 Sol. The coalition included partners such as Wiz and Cloudflare, focusing on preparing fixes, testing, and deploying protections ahead of public disclosure to mitigate widespread risk. The initiative, called Patch the Planet, involved validating vulnerabilities, developing patches, and coordinating with infrastructure providers and government agencies to protect critical systems. OpenAI also committed $1 billion in subsidized AI model access to support frontline defenders with limited security resources. This effort highlights both the potential and risks of AI in cybersecurity, as AI can uncover flaws faster than attackers but also accelerate exploit development. OpenAI proposes a scalable framework for coordinated vulnerability response in the AI era, emphasizing collaboration among maintainers, researchers, providers, and governments to manage the increasing pace of AI-discovered security issues in widely used software.

items.title: Report: Texas data center expansion could triple soot and double smog pollution by 2031, reversing decades of air quality improvements [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: A surge in new data centers in Texas, driven by demand for generative AI infrastructure, could significantly increase air pollution to levels not seen since the early 2000s. The Houston Advanced Research Center (HARC) warns that if these data centers rely on the current electricity grid mix, emissions of fine particle pollution and smog-forming nitrogen oxides could more than double within five years, erasing years of air quality progress. Texas leads the US in data center capacity with 26 gigawatts existing or under construction and is expected to add more onsite power generation, often using gas turbines that are less efficient and more polluting. HARC's modeling shows that pairing grid power with onsite renewable energy could reduce emissions substantially, but reliance on gas engines could result in the highest pollution scenarios. The report highlights the risk that air quality gains achieved over decades could be undone if cleaner energy solutions are not prioritized in data center development.

items.title: OpenAI updates Usage Policies and aligns safety standards with partners to ensure consistent safeguards across services offering GPT-6 Astra and other models [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: OpenAI has worked with customers and partners to align safety policies across services providing access to its models, including GPT-6 Astra, and is updating its Usage Policies effective November 20, 2026, to clarify rules for safe AI development and sensitive uses. The company evaluates model risks before deployment, monitors for misuse, and requires partners to maintain safeguards consistent with OpenAI's standards, investigating violations and coordinating enforcement across platforms. OpenAI is also introducing SafetyIDs to help identify misuse more precisely while protecting user privacy, aiming to support responsible access and clear expectations for developers and businesses using its AI models.

items.title: Alter launches privileged access management platform for AI agents with per-agent keys, policy enforcement, and audit trails [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Alter has introduced a privileged access management platform designed for AI agents that enables control over agent actions on behalf of users. The platform provides per-agent identities and scoped credentials, enforces policies including human approvals, and maintains tamper-evident audit logs for every action. The system stores credentials securely in a vault and injects them per request, preventing exposure in code or environment files. It supports integrations with LangChain, MCP, and AWS, and offers features such as default-deny policies, instant revocation, and compliance-ready audit trails. Alter aims to help teams pass security reviews and maintain strict access controls for multi-user AI agents.

items.title: LiteLLM patches security breach after attacker pushed malware in v1.107.0 Docker and PyPI releases on October 21, 2026 [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: LiteLLM confirmed a security incident on October 21, 2026, when its release pipeline was compromised, resulting in a malicious v1.107.0 version being published to Docker Hub and PyPI. This version contained malware designed to steal credentials and enable remote code execution. The affected releases were live for a limited time before being pulled, and all previous versions remain safe. Enterprise customers using the private LiteLLM registry were not impacted. The compromised artifacts included multiple Docker images and PyPI packages available between approximately 11:39 and 14:20 UTC. LiteLLM identified the attack chain involved multiple security control breaches. Users who installed or ran the affected versions are advised to assume compromise, remove malicious files, and downgrade to version 1.106.2 or earlier. The company continues investigating the incident and has provided detailed guidance for detection and remediation.

items.title: Meta restructures stock influenced by Mark Zuckerberg's concerns over California wealth tax and capital needs
items.content_text: Meta Platforms restructured its stock to address anticipated capital requirements and concerns about a proposed wealth tax in California that could impact CEO Mark Zuckerberg's financial interests. These considerations played a key role in the company's decision to overhaul its stock structure.

items.title: HN Sieve launches AI tool to score and summarize every Show HN post on Hacker News [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: HN Sieve is a new tool that uses artificial intelligence to evaluate and summarize every Show HN post on Hacker News, offering users concise insights and assessments of the projects showcased. The platform aims to help users quickly understand the value and relevance of submissions by providing AI-generated scores and summaries.

items.title: AT&T partners with OpenAI to enhance in-house legal work by improving knowledge access and automating intake processes for faster, more informed legal judgment [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: AT&T is collaborating with OpenAI to advance its LegalEdge initiative, aiming to streamline how its in-house legal team accesses expertise and manages incoming requests. The partnership focuses on building a natural language intake system that classifies and prioritizes legal matters, connects them with relevant precedents, and provides context to lawyers to improve efficiency. This system is designed to reduce the time lawyers spend gathering information, allowing them to focus more on applying their judgment. AT&T emphasizes that final decision-making authority remains with its legal professionals, while the technology supports better-informed and scalable legal advice across the company.

items.title: Amazon warns of new AI-discovered cybersecurity flaws being widely exploited [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Amazon has issued a warning about recently identified cybersecurity vulnerabilities that are being broadly exploited. These flaws were detected with the help of artificial intelligence, underscoring AI's increasing role in both discovering and potentially enabling exploitation of security weaknesses.

items.title: Meta, Sierra, and partners launch Personal Agent Protocol to standardize secure interactions between personal AI agents and businesses [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Meta, Sierra, and industry partners including Genesys, Instinct, Rocket, Shopify, Stripe, and Walmart have introduced the Personal Agent Protocol, an open standard designed to enable personal AI agents to interact securely and efficiently with businesses. The protocol aims to improve interoperability by allowing consumers to control agent access while giving companies visibility and control over agent actions through websites, APIs, or company agents. The protocol uses OAuth for authorization and supports multiple connection methods, including websites, APIs built on standards like MCP and OpenAPI, and conversational agents for complex tasks. It is designed to enhance user experience by speeding up tasks such as scheduling, shopping, and customer support, while maintaining privacy and security. The developers plan to publish the initial specification and reference implementation soon and invite further collaboration to expand features like detailed permissions, push notifications, and payment extensions.

items.title: Timeline details PHP2Shell vulnerability leak and embargo break from discovery to public disclosure
items.content_text: A detailed timeline documents the sequence of events surrounding the PHP2Shell vulnerability leak and embargo break, covering the initial discovery, efforts to coordinate responsible disclosure, and the unauthorized release of information. This chronology highlights key moments that affected the security community's ability to respond effectively to the vulnerability.

items.title: Microsoft warns of Chinese state-linked cyberattacks using AI agent Artex targeting hundreds of organizations since September [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Microsoft has reported that a Chinese state-linked cyber threat actor known as Storm-0940 has been conducting automated cyberattacks powered by an AI agent called Artex. These attacks have targeted hundreds of organizations worldwide across various industries since September, illustrating the growing use of artificial intelligence in cyber threats.

items.title: Discussion on AI's ability to generate reliable product demos directly from source code, highlighting challenges in workflow understanding and UI synchronization [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: A recent discussion on Hacker News explores whether artificial intelligence can reliably generate product demonstrations directly from source code. The conversation focuses on the difficulties of interpreting application workflows, identifying meaningful user interface states, and synchronizing animations with narration to create effective demos. These challenges highlight the complexity of automating demo creation despite advances in AI technology.

items.title: Researchers demonstrate how a malicious webpage can hijack AI agents by exploiting web interactions, highlighting security vulnerabilities [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: The article examines the risk that malicious webpages pose to AI agents by potentially hijacking their operations through web-based interactions. It highlights how AI agents, when processing web content, may be vulnerable to exploitation if adequate security measures are not implemented. The discussion underscores the need for robust safeguards to prevent unauthorized manipulation or control of AI systems via web interfaces.

items.title: OpenAI-led coalition addresses critical PHP vulnerabilities as US Super Intelligence Force coordinates AI cybersecurity response amid tech industry updates [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: A coalition led by OpenAI is focusing on patching critical vulnerabilities in PHP, emphasizing the shrinking "defender's window" for cybersecurity fixes before exploitation. The U.S. government has formed the Super Intelligence Force to coordinate responses to AI-related cybersecurity threats, marking its first major collaboration with OpenAI on a recent vulnerability. In parallel, Meta reported strong third-quarter revenue growth and introduced a new stock class to fund AI investments without diluting CEO Mark Zuckerberg's control, despite ongoing legal expenses. Tesla's revenues remained flat with a slight decline in automotive revenue, and CEO Elon Musk avoided discussing a potential SpaceX merger. Additional industry developments include Electronic Arts planning job cuts and studio closure, Microsoft's CEO pay reduction proposal, and Google's decision to stop requiring nondisclosure agreements from local officials for data center projects.

items.title: Notcho launches AI agent running on a private cloud computer in your device's notch, using your Claude Pro or Max plan [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Notcho has introduced an AI agent named Claude Code that operates from the notch area of a Windows device, running on its own private Linux desktop in the cloud. The agent performs tasks independently using the user's Claude Pro or Max subscription, handling activities like booking trips, managing inboxes, and building spreadsheets without accessing the user's local system resources. Users install a Windows app that pairs their device with the agent's cloud computer, allowing them to monitor progress or intervene when necessary. The service includes features such as scheduled routines, chat history, and secure login storage, with a pricing model of $14.99 per month after a seven-day free trial. Notcho emphasizes privacy by keeping all activity on the agent's cloud computer and never accessing user passwords or local files.

items.title: Blackstone's Jas Khaira says concerns over AI infrastructure debt are exaggerated amid rising interest rates and market jitters [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Blackstone is heavily investing in AI infrastructure through its Blackstone N1 group, led by Jas Khaira, who emphasizes the firm's unique approach to financing AI compute with flexible capital structures. Despite recent market concerns about the large debt burdens of AI-focused neocloud providers like CoreWeave and Firmus, Khaira argues that fears are overblown, citing strong customer contracts and the ongoing high demand for compute resources. Khaira explained that rising interest rates and credit spreads have increased borrowing costs even for major tech companies, contributing to market volatility and the cancellation of Firmus' IPO. However, Blackstone continues to support AI infrastructure buildout, viewing its $1.3 trillion in assets as critical to meeting the capital-intensive needs of the AI transition.

items.title: Nokia, T-Mobile, and Nvidia complete world's first AI-RAN call, demonstrating AI integration in mobile network infrastructure [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Nokia, T-Mobile, and Nvidia have successfully completed the first call using an Artificial Intelligence Radio Access Network (AI-RAN), marking a significant step in applying AI technologies to enhance mobile network performance and efficiency. This collaboration showcases the potential for AI to optimize radio access networks, potentially improving connectivity and resource management in future mobile communications.

items.title: OpenAI urges California Governor Newsom to strengthen AI regulations with mandatory shutdown controls, annual audits, and enhanced cybersecurity [ * ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: OpenAI has called on California Governor Gavin Newsom to enhance AI regulatory measures by requiring mandatory shutdown controls for AI models, conducting annual independent audits, and improving cybersecurity standards. The company specifically recommends bolstering Senate Bill 53 to ensure more effective oversight and safety in AI development.

items.title: Lumen launches AI desktop overlay for real-time problem solving and code debugging with privacy features on Windows and macOS [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Lumen has introduced an AI overlay application that integrates directly onto Windows 10/11 and macOS desktops, allowing users to press a hotkey to capture screen content and receive explanations, solutions, or summaries without switching windows. The tool supports debugging code, solving math problems, and summarizing text by analyzing selected screen areas and providing actionable answers instantly. The overlay remains invisible during screen sharing or recordings by using native OS features to exclude itself from capture on platforms like Zoom and Microsoft Teams. Lumen offers a free tier with limited daily requests and a Pro subscription with increased capacity, advanced AI reasoning, and enhanced privacy through a Stealth Mode that hides the overlay completely during video calls and recordings.

items.title: Meta says Muse AI app has over 10 million users with shopping as a leading activity, average purchase over $200 [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Meta reported during its Q3 earnings call that its AI app Muse has surpassed 10 million users, with about 25% of new users engaging daily. CEO Mark Zuckerberg highlighted that shopping is a major use case, with over a quarter of engaged shoppers making purchases averaging more than $200. Zuckerberg noted that Muse also supports personal productivity tasks like email and calendar integration, emphasizing user trust in its security features. Meta plans to scale Muse, improve cost efficiency, and expects the app to generate higher revenue per user than its existing family of apps. The company aims to monetize Muse primarily through commerce commissions and premium AI model access while forecasting profitability as usage grows.

items.title: Report: AI agent deletes entire edit of Swedish TV show The Challenge weeks before release due to failed backup system [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: The Swedish edition of the athletic competition show The Challenge lost months of editing work when an AI agent deleted the finished season from the production server just weeks before its release. The program director attributed the incident to a failed backup system, which prevented recovery of the deleted files and forced the production team to re-edit the entire season from raw footage. According to sources cited by Aftonbladet, the AI agent had file-handling permissions on the production server and deleted the completed edit, though the exact role of the AI agent remains unclear. TV4, the show's commissioner, conducted an investigation and stated the mishap was due to human error rather than autonomous AI action. The incident highlights risks associated with AI file management and backup failures in media production environments.

items.title: Russia intensifies crackdown on aggressive bears amid rising real attacks causing public fear
items.content_text: Russian authorities have increased efforts to manage incidents involving bears exhibiting aggressive behavior, which have heightened public concern. The government has implemented enhanced safety measures and monitoring to prevent further attacks and address the growing fear among communities.

items.title: OpenAI expands ChatGPT Ads to 26 new countries, reaching 89 countries worldwide with over 100,000 advertisers using the platform [ * ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: OpenAI has expanded ChatGPT Ads to 26 additional countries, increasing its availability to 89 countries globally and attracting over 100,000 advertisers since its launch eight months ago. The ads appear only on the Free and Go plans, while Pro and Enterprise subscriptions remain ad-free, supporting free and low-cost access to ChatGPT. The expansion includes new markets across Latin America, Europe, the Middle East, Africa, and Asia, allowing businesses of all sizes to reach users as they explore and compare options within ChatGPT. OpenAI emphasizes privacy and transparency by keeping conversations private from advertisers and clearly labeling ads separate from ChatGPT's responses. Looking ahead, OpenAI plans to develop additional ad formats, objectives, buying options, and measurement tools to enhance business interactions with consumers on ChatGPT, aiming to help users discover relevant products and services while supporting business growth.

items.title: Nvidia expands multibillion-dollar deals with six chip substrate suppliers including Ibiden, Samsung Electro-Mechanics, and Unimicron to secure AI server chip production [ * ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Nvidia announced new agreements with six chip substrate suppliers, including Ibiden, Samsung Electro-Mechanics, and Unimicron, to ensure sufficient component materials for increased production of its AI server chips in the coming years. These deals involve multibillion-dollar reservations aimed at stabilizing Nvidia's supply chain amid growing demand for AI hardware.

items.title: Meta plans new non-voting share class to fund AI initiatives, acquisitions, and employee compensation starting in 2027 [ * ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Meta announced it will issue a new class of non-voting shares to finance its AI projects, potential acquisitions, and employee compensation, with trading expected to begin in 2027. The move was disclosed as part of Meta's third-quarter earnings report, highlighting the significant investment needed to compete and grow amid the AI industry transformation. The company expects capital expenditures between $135 billion and $145 billion this year, up from previous estimates, reflecting its heavy investment in AI infrastructure, talent acquisition, and model development. Meta recently launched its AI agent Muse, which has gained rapid user adoption despite some privacy concerns and feature pauses.

items.title: Recursive launches Flint, a free laptop-sized coding model largely developed by its AI research system, as an early test of AI self-improvement [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Recursive, an AI startup founded last year, has released Flint, a free coding model designed to run on laptops that was largely built using its own AI research system called the Eureka Machine. This model represents an early public test of recursive self-improvement, where AI assists in building better AI under human supervision. Flint uses a mixture-of-experts architecture with 40 billion parameters but activates only 2.5 billion at a time, making it lightweight enough for ordinary laptops. It outperforms similar-sized models on coding benchmarks and runs faster on devices like the MacBook Pro with Apple's M4 Pro chip. Recursive aims for the Eureka Machine to progressively improve its research capabilities, potentially enabling more autonomous AI development in the future while maintaining human oversight.

items.title: Databricks launches AI Runtime with managed GPU infrastructure for scalable, secure enterprise AI model training [ * ] [ ⬢ ]
items.content_text: Databricks has launched AI Runtime (AIR), a managed service that integrates high-performance GPU infrastructure directly into its platform to enable scalable and secure training of AI models on enterprise data. AIR aims to reduce operational overhead by providing serverless, on-demand GPU access with built-in governance through Unity Catalog, allowing teams to focus on model development without managing GPU infrastructure separately. The service offers features such as near-instant launch latency, environment caching, and debugging tools compatible with major AI frameworks including Ray. Hundreds of companies across industries like healthcare and manufacturing are already using AIR to accelerate deep learning model training and deployment. AIR also integrates with Databricks' Lakeflow for pipeline orchestration and supports multi-node training with optimized performance and workload isolation to protect sensitive data.

items.title: Stanford HAI develops method to track AI's real-time impact on labor market employment trends [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Stanford HAI has created a method to monitor how artificial intelligence affects the labor market in real time, offering insights into AI's influence on employment patterns and job dynamics. This approach aims to provide up-to-date data on the evolving relationship between AI technologies and workforce changes, helping to understand the broader economic and social implications of AI adoption.

items.title: Meta creates new Class C non-voting shares to raise capital for AI investments while preserving CEO Zuckerberg's voting control [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Meta Platforms announced a new class of non-voting Class C common stock to facilitate fundraising for its AI initiatives without diluting CEO Mark Zuckerberg's voting power. The move was revealed alongside the company's quarterly financial results and aims to support Meta's aggressive investment strategy in artificial intelligence.

items.title: Walmart launches Agent Gateway to enable AI agents to shop with user controls, contrasting Amazon's ban on AI agent purchases [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Walmart has introduced its Agent Gateway, a new platform allowing AI agents to make purchases on behalf of customers with spending controls and transaction approvals. This move follows Amazon's decision to block AI agents from shopping on its site, positioning Walmart as a leader in agentic commerce. The Agent Gateway uses the model context protocol to connect approved AI agents to Walmart's inventory, enabling shopping without sharing personal data directly with the agents. Walmart also plans to roll out Agent Profiles that let customers authorize agents, monitor purchases separately, and set spending limits or approval requirements. Walmart's approach includes specific terms for AI agents to ensure they act within customer intentions, restrict access to payment information, and comply with return policies. Agents violating these terms will be blocked, aiming to provide a secure and user-friendly experience as AI-driven shopping becomes more mainstream.

items.title: Court rules Elon Musk's ex-girlfriend must face countersuit in xAI forum
items.content_text: A court has ruled that Elon Musk's ex-girlfriend must respond to a countersuit filed in the xAI forum, advancing a legal dispute involving the AI company and the former partner. The case involves claims and counterclaims between the parties related to their interactions and the company.

items.title: Anthropic launches Claude Duet AI agent for professionals and small businesses as a research preview on iOS, Android, and web [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Anthropic has introduced Claude Duet, a new AI agent designed for professionals and small business owners, available as a research preview. The agent operates on Claude Opus 5.5 and can manage tasks ranging from scheduling meetings to building dashboards and financial forecasts, sending users daily briefs and alerts only when necessary. Claude Duet integrates memory, skills, and connected apps from Claude and includes a virtual machine with browsing capabilities. It requires user approval before performing sensitive actions and employs a safety system to protect sensitive information like credit card numbers. Currently, it is an early version with some limitations, such as occasional misreading of priorities and weaker performance on personal errands. Access is limited to Pro or Max subscribers in the US via a waitlist.

items.title: Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg agrees to remain in California for eight years under new stock agreement amid potential billionaire tax ballot measure [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg has agreed to stay in California for eight years despite considering a move due to a proposed ballot measure that would impose a one-time 5 percent tax on billionaires' stock and assets. The agreement, reached with Meta's board, links his ability to sell special nonvoting shares to his continued residence in the state, aiming to keep him close to the company's AI development efforts in Silicon Valley. The decision follows concerns from a special committee of Meta's board about the challenges faced when Zuckerberg was not physically present during the COVID-19 pandemic. The new class of shares created under the agreement could help fund Meta's AI investments without diluting Zuckerberg's voting control. While the agreement allows for relocation if Meta moves its headquarters, recent polling suggests the tax measure may not pass, potentially reducing the immediate tax impact on Zuckerberg.

items.title: Researchers develop multi-agent large language model system to coordinate and play Pokémon Showdown 2v2 battles, demonstrating improved performance with agent communication [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers have created a multi-agent environment using large language models (LLMs) to play Pokémon Showdown's 2v2 format, focusing on how agents coordinate, communicate, and strategize together. The system allows agents to exchange messages and choose moves based on a plain-English summary of the battle, aiming to evaluate collaborative behaviors in a game-theory setting with hidden information and randomness. Experiments showed that agents who communicated freely won 64% of battles against a scripted max-damage bot, outperforming agents with limited or no communication. The environment uses the official Pokémon Showdown simulator and supports different communication modes, serving as a benchmark for comparing model capabilities and potentially training agents with reinforcement learning to enhance collaboration. The project highlights the importance of agent interaction in multi-agent AI systems and plans to develop a leaderboard and further research on communication effects.

items.title: Thoma Bravo-backed Proofpoint to acquire Varonis Systems for $6.3 billion at a discount amid rising cybersecurity M&A activity [ * ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Thoma Bravo's cybersecurity firm Proofpoint agreed to acquire data security company Varonis Systems for $6.3 billion, valuing Varonis at about six times forward annual recurring revenue, below comparable public peers. This deal highlights how private equity can still find opportunities in the competitive cybersecurity market despite rising interest rates and high corporate acquisition activity. The acquisition expands Proofpoint's offerings beyond email threat protection to include data security and access control, positioning it for potential future growth and an IPO. The deal is expected to close in the first half of 2027, with Thoma Bravo planning additional large cybersecurity acquisitions focused on AI-driven revenue models.

items.title: Walmart to allow AI agents to shop on its website with user approval and spending limits starting next month [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Walmart will enable customers to use AI agents to shop on its website beginning next month, implementing controls that require user approval for purchases and allow setting spending limits. The company has established rules to ensure AI agents act only within the shopper's intent and restrict access to necessary information, blocking agents that violate these terms. This move contrasts with Amazon's approach, which has blocked similar AI shopping assistants. Walmart's system includes an "Agent Gateway" that connects AI agents through an open standard called the Model Context Protocol, facilitating smoother shopping experiences without exposing customers' full shopping histories. Users can manage AI agent activity through "Agent Profiles," reviewing purchases separately and disabling agents at any time. The feature will also be available on Sam's Club, reflecting Walmart's broader embrace of AI shopping assistants while maintaining user control and privacy.

items.title: NSA warns of critical PHP vulnerabilities found by OpenAI and Google's Wiz, urging immediate patching of millions of websites [ ! ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: The U.S. National Security Agency issued a warning about two severe security flaws in PHP, a server-side language powering about 70% of websites, including WordPress sites. These vulnerabilities, present since PHP version 5 released in 2004, allow attackers to access server file systems or databases, prompting the NSA to recommend taking unpatched sites offline until fixed. OpenAI and Google's Wiz discovered the flaws using AI tools as part of responsible security research, collaborating with the PHP Foundation and major tech companies to develop and test patches. While no exploits have been reported yet, AI now lowers the barrier for attackers to adapt exploits across PHP versions, making rapid patching critical to protect millions of websites from potential attacks.

items.title: Judge denies Trump administration's motion to dismiss NAACP lawsuit against xAI, allowing case to proceed [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: A judge has rejected the Trump administration's request to dismiss a lawsuit filed by the NAACP against xAI, an artificial intelligence company. This decision permits the legal action to continue in court. The lawsuit involves allegations related to xAI's activities, though specific claims were not detailed in the report.

items.title: Anthropic CEO says competing in AI development can promote stronger safety measures [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Anthropic's CEO has argued that the competitive race to develop artificial intelligence technologies can serve as a strategy to improve safety in the field. He suggests that this competition encourages the adoption of robust safety protocols and responsible innovation practices. This perspective highlights a view that advancing AI capabilities through competition may incentivize better safety standards rather than compromise them.

items.title: Blacksmith raises $66 million Series C led by Sequoia, reaches $1 billion valuation as AI-driven code testing demand grows [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Blacksmith, a platform that helps companies build and test AI-generated software more efficiently, announced a $66 million Series C funding round led by Sequoia that values the company at $1 billion. The company aims to simplify continuous integration (CI) processes amid increasing volumes of AI-written code. Blacksmith reported a 17-fold increase in annual recurring revenue and has processed over 90 million CI jobs, with customers including Mercury and Granola. This Series C follows a $45 million Series B two months earlier, which valued the company at $550 million, marking rapid growth since its $60 million valuation a year ago.

items.title: SZED submits multi-task label-attention and cross-modal fusion model for Arabic hateful meme detection in ArGuard 2026 Track A [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: SZED presented their model for the ArGuard 2026 Track A challenge on Arabic hateful meme detection, which involves binary classification and fine-grained multi-label tagging. Their approach combines MARBERTv2 and CLIP ViT-L/14 embeddings for classification and uses a multi-task label-attention architecture with per-class query vectors and cascade calibration for tagging, achieving macro-F1 scores of 0.7597 and 0.3142 respectively. The team compared different fusion methods including concatenation, self-attention, and ensemble heads for the classification task and analyzed reproducibility, per-class error patterns, and the impact of cascade calibration on the long-tailed label distribution in the tagging task.

items.title: Researchers introduce MEDIATOR, an ontology-agnostic tokenizer for EHR modeling that improves clinical prediction and zero-shot transfer across health systems [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Researchers present MEDIATOR, a discrete tokenizer that maps clinical concepts from text into a shared vector-quantized codebook, enabling open-vocabulary tokenization without manual mappings or fixed vocabularies. MEDIATOR addresses the tokenization bottleneck in electronic health record (EHR) foundation models by collapsing equivalent expressions and organizing distinct concepts in a medically meaningful discrete space. When used with an EHR Transformer, MEDIATOR improves prediction accuracy on 20 MIMIC-III tasks and shows significant gains in zero-shot transfer to 14 eICU tasks, utilizing all events where previous models could only use a fraction. The model's design enhances transfer robustness, entity-linking quality, and enables transferable attribution across hospitals, supporting scalable clinical prediction across diverse health systems.

items.title: Researchers propose ICLHerd, a herding-based data selection method for large language models that balances mode-seeking and mode-averaging using the von Mises-Fisher kernel and in-context learning as a validation proxy [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Data selection critically impacts large language model training quality and downstream performance. Existing methods that select data based on maximum similarity to a development set tend to cluster tightly around those samples, causing mode-seeking bias. The proposed ICLHerd framework addresses this by using the von Mises-Fisher kernel to balance mode-seeking with mode-averaging and employs in-context learning as a proxy for efficient hyperparameter tuning. Experiments show that ICLHerd outperforms previous data selection algorithms, underscoring the importance of balancing these selection strategies for improved model training.

items.title: Researchers identify implicit token budgeting causing error increase in language models when composing multiple tasks, affecting models like Claude Opus 5 [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers have found that modern language models make significantly more errors when handling multiple tasks in a single prompt compared to solving each task individually. This error increase is linked to an implicit token budget that reduces the tokens allocated per task during composition, even when the total prompt length is within the model's context window. Tasks requiring longer reasoning are particularly fragile under composition, leading to more mistakes, while simpler tasks receive excess tokens when isolated, wasting compute. The study analyzed both open-weight models and the Claude Opus 5 model, showing that by grouping tasks based on their fragility, it is possible to manipulate this implicit budgeting to reduce token usage by 43% across various math and linguistic tasks without sacrificing accuracy. This finding highlights a fundamental limitation in current language model task composition and suggests strategies for more efficient multi-task prompting.

items.title: Researchers present Symbolic Preference Labeling to audit AI safety preference supervision with recorded derivations enabling inspection without rerunning models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers introduce Symbolic Preference Labeling, a method where a pretrained language model classifies attributes of prompts and responses, and explicit rules assign verdicts to generate preference labels with recorded derivations. This approach allows preference labels and verdicts to be recomputed from stored data without rerunning the model, enhancing transparency in preference supervision. In experiments on 200 human-annotated prompts, the model produced valid structured outputs for 192, with parsing failures occurring only in harmful self-harm prompts. Using 465 preference pairs, a policy model was trained showing a mean benign refusal rate of 40.82% on 1,319 benign prompts resembling unsafe ones, and a toxic refusal rate of 84.98% on 655 toxic prompts. The study distinguishes reproducibility of preference labels from attribute correctness, noting that while recorded derivations enable inspection, separate validation is needed for attribute accuracy and semantic safety.

items.title: Researchers find large language models often bypass English safety filters when responding in low-resource languages, with bypass rates between 21.9% and 44.4% across 78 languages [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: A study evaluated ten widely used large language models (LLMs) across 79 languages, including English and 78 low-resource languages, to assess safety alignment. The research found that harmful requests blocked in English could still produce unsafe outputs when translated into other languages, revealing significant safety bypass risks concentrated in certain language families. The study also noted that model rankings based on bypass rates were unstable across different evaluation methods, indicating variability in how models handle translation-related safety issues.

items.title: Researchers find that mixture-of-experts model routers inherently encode expert selection information, reducing the need for separate sparse dictionaries in large language models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers studied mixture-of-experts (MoE) models and found that the router component, which selects experts for processing tokens, already contains information that a sparse dictionary would otherwise need to learn. Using an expert-aligned autoencoder on a 26-billion-parameter model after training on ten million tokens, they showed that the router explains a significant portion of variance in expert outputs compared to various control models. The study noted that each expert writes into a subspace of the model, linking expert identity to subspace representation, but did not measure how much this explains. The implementation did not improve training speed, and aspects like semantic interpretability and causal faithfulness remain untested.

items.title: Researchers introduce learned readout tokens to improve confidence estimation in large language models, outperforming existing-token probes across multiple datasets and models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers propose a new method called ScratchProbe that learns a dedicated readout token to extract confidence scores from large language models (LLMs), improving prediction of output correctness. This approach surpasses traditional probes that rely on existing vocabulary tokens and can be extended to multiple tokens for further gains. The method is compatible with existing probes and enhances performance metrics such as AUROC both within and outside the training domain.

items.title: Factual Access States in Diffusion Language Models: From Mechanism to Knowledge Editing and Retrieval [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.27580v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Factual recall is a lookup: some representation inside the network serves as the key, and what that key is made of decides which queries can retrieve the fact, what an edit must cover, and what a retriever can read. We call it the factual access state. In autoregressive (AR) models the subject position enriches attributes largely independently of the relation, and relation-specific selection happens later, at the readout position. In masked diffusion language models (DLMs) we find the state is assembled differently, and much earlier: in the first attention layer the wording of the relation is routed into the position of whichever entity is visible and the early feed-forward layers look the fact up on this fused representation. The state therefore varies with the relation's surface form and with the query direction, so the queries about one fact occupy a region of state space rather than a point, and an operation on the fact succeeds only for queries that enter it. We treat the state as an interface to a DLM's factual knowledge, and put it to two uses. Writing to the state gives a knowledge editor: from one declarative statement, Multi-View Edit fits one shared value per direction across that region and installs it in the early-MLP block, preserving source-prompt reliability while substantially improving paraphrase and reverse question answering, where AR editors gain near zero. Reading it suggests a complementary use: the state at each entity position can serve as a relation-specific retrieval vector with no training, returning both pieces of evidence for two-entity queries on which pooled, prompted and lexical retrievers almost never return both.

items.title: On-Policy Transition Distillation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.28048v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) consolidates expert capabilities into a single student by matching teacher and student final-layer distributions on student-generated rollouts. We investigate whether depthwise prediction transitions, the changes in predictions between layers, can provide additional task-relevant supervision. Our diagnostic study finds that stronger teacher--student agreement in intermediate transitions is associated with higher answer correctness within questions, with correct responses exhibiting lower mean transition KL across all measured intermediate layer pairs. These observations motivate On-Policy Transition Distillation (OPTD), which augments final-layer distribution matching by aligning teacher and student layer-to-layer log-probability increments on student-generated rollouts. Evaluations across three backbones and eight benchmarks spanning mathematics, coding, and instruction following show that OPTD achieves the best or tied-best overall performance in both dual- and three-domain distillation. In the three-domain setting, OPTD recovers $\approx 90\%$ of the overall teacher--student capability gap, compared with $\approx 75\%$ for OPD.

items.title: BitMTP: When Multi-Token Prediction Meets Low-Bit Large Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.28500v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: For efficient deployment of large language models (LLMs), methods of ultra-low-bit backbones reduce weight storage, memory traffic, and linear-layer execution cost, while multi-token prediction (MTP) methods reduce sequential decoding steps by predicting multiple future tokens in parallel. Although complementary, the direct combination of these methods cannot accelerate decoding at comparable quality: masked drafting lacks intermediate token input supplied in next-token training, while wider computation and causal key-value (KV) updates can offset the savings from fewer steps. To address these challenges, we propose BitMTP, an algorithm-system co-design framework for efficient MTP on ultra-low-bit LLM backbones. A joint next-token prediction and MTP objective equips a single model with both autoregressive (AR) generation and block-causal drafting. Confidence-only decoding, speculative-only decoding, and hybrid decoding provide different quality-throughput operating points without using separate draft and verifier models. Accepted-prefix alignment keeps the committed prefix, materialized causal KV boundary, and CUDA Graph replay state consistent for continued generation. BitMTP uses this contract to select width-specialized low-bit execution and reuse captured graphs over shared KV storage. On NVIDIA H20, BitMTP with hybrid decoding achieves five-task mean speedups of 2.2x on BitNet b1.58-2B and 2.1-2.4x on 1.7B-4B Bonsai models at comparable task quality. On RTX 3090 and Jetson Orin, it further achieves up to 2.0x in five-task mean throughput and 3.3x on MBPP+, respectively. These results demonstrate that BitMTP accelerates ultra-low-bit LLM generation across backbones, model sizes, and GPU types. The source code is released at https://github.com/PolyU-VCLab/BitMTP

items.title: ReuF2F: Benchmarking Coding Agents on Formalized Undergraduate Research Problems [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.27046v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As AI systems begin to resolve open research problems, reliable verification becomes increasingly important. Formal mathematics provides a trusted framework for mathematical reasoning, enabling agents to produce machine-checkable proofs while conducting mathematical exploration. Existing formal mathematics benchmarks often focus on known results or a small set of prominent open problems, which can become difficult to evaluate reliably once solutions are discovered and widely disseminated. Existing evaluation protocols are also not always aligned with how modern coding agents operate. We therefore introduce ReuF2F, a Lean 4 benchmark of 244 formalized open problems drawn from Research Experiences for Undergraduates (REU), spanning entry-level open research problems across a broad range of mathematical subfields. We expect these less prominent open problems, which tend to attract less attention and may remain unsolved for longer, to be better suited for held-out evaluation of end-to-end open problem resolution in Lean. We adopt a standard coding-agent evaluation setting, placing each problem and its logical negation into a Lean project in a Docker container. We also build Leanimum-agent on mini-SWE-agent to provide a unified harness for fair comparisons across models. Our evaluation finds that even the best-performing model resolves only ~40% of the problems, leaving substantial room for improvement on formalized open research problems.

items.title: TxnQA: Benchmarking Analytical Reasoning and Evidence Grounding over Transaction Event Sequences [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.27256v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Analyzing merchant transaction histories requires dynamic temporal filtering, entity resolution, and aggregation over irregular event streams--operations poorly captured by static tabular or time-series forecasting benchmarks. We introduce TxnQA, an analytical QA benchmark comprising 27 task families (81 templates) alongside a 5-scenario fraud-risk reasoning suite that evaluates both verdicts and supporting evidence over synthetic, privacy-mitigated transaction data. Ground-truth answers are computed programmatically, and model performance is decomposed into format-following rate (FFR), conditional content accuracy (CA), and end-to-end correctness (E2E). Evaluating prompted proprietary baselines and six LoRA-adapted open-weight models shows that adaptation reliably enforces output schemas but leaves arithmetic bottlenecks: Gemma-4-31B-IT and Qwen3-8B attain E2E scores of 0.867 and 0.816, whereas evaluated MoE checkpoints reach only 0.632-0.713. Furthermore, on the 500-instance fraud suite, verdict accuracy frequently exceeds 80%, yet joint accuracy (requiring exact evidence attribution) collapses to at most ~23%. These findings identify schema compliance, semantic calculation, and evidence attribution as three distinct bottlenecks in transaction-sequence QA.

items.title: TEX: Test-Time Scaling Testing Agents via Execution-based Cross-Validation [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.27290v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Test-case generation is critical but remains challenging for language models. Existing test-time scaling methods either isolate candidates or aggregate traces, which do not scale to long-horizon tasks. We present TEX, a collaborative test-time scaling framework based on execution-driven cross-validation. TEX parallelizes agents to generate tests and patches, cross-executing each test against every patch to form a $K \times K$ feedback matrix. Agents use their matrix slices for refinement, enabling objective validation without verbose trace sharing. On SWT-Bench Verified, TEX achieves 86.4%, establishing a new state-of-the-art and improving +9.0% over single-agent baselines. Moreover, even random selection from TEX outputs (84.4%) surpasses the previous SOTA (84.0%), showing collaborative execution feedback improves solution quality, not just best-case samples. Our results highlight execution-grounded feedback as an effective scaling mechanism for long-horizon agentic tasks.

items.title: Self-Evolving Agents through Privileged Retrospective Distillation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.27495v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Self-evolving agents aim to improve from their own experience rather than remain fixed after deployment, but naturally collected trajectories often lack ground-truth solutions or verifier-derived rewards. We introduce Retrospective Self-Distillation (RSD), a multi-round framework that turns such experience into dense supervision using privileged retrospective context. For each on-policy trajectory, the same underlying model acts as both student and teacher: the teacher re-scores the student's realized actions while conditioning on cross-task precedents and lessons, together with turn-level reflection and future hindsight from the completed trajectory. The resulting teacher distribution is distilled back into the policy through on-policy self-distillation. Across rounds, the experience bank grows and the retrospective context is refreshed, allowing the model, its data, and its supervision to co-evolve. We further introduce frontier-guided context-policy evolution, where a stronger frontier model proposes constrained edits to how privileged context is constructed. Across ALFWorld, ScienceWorld, and SearchQA with Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-14B, RSD improves performance by up to 59.7% relative to the base model, while frontier-guided context-policy evolution adds up to a further 44.7% relative improvement over a fixed context policy. These results show that naturally accumulated experience can be converted into persistent model capability without ground-truth trajectories or verifier-derived rewards for the core policy update.

items.title: Can Native Safety Travel? Reusing Safety Pretraining Across Models via On-Policy Distillation [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.27555v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Safety pretraining has emerged as a promising paradigm for embedding safety deeply into a model during pretraining, yielding robustness to subsequent fine-tuning that conventional safety post-training often lacks. We refer to this safety acquired during model pretraining as native safety. Yet native safety is expensive to acquire, confined to the model in which it was pretrained, and often accompanied by lower general utility. In this work, we rethink the practical value of safety-pretrained models and introduce, for the first time, the native safety reuse problem: Can native safety be transferred from a specialized, potentially smaller, safety-pretrained "teacher" to standard-pretrained "students," enabling them to inherit its robustness while preserving their general utility? We show that native safety can "travel" through on-policy distillation. A standard-pretrained student generates responses to safety-pretraining prompts, while a small safety-pretrained teacher supervises the student's token-level predictions along its own generated trajectories; cross-tokenizer alignment further enables transfer across model families. The resulting students exhibit substantially greater safety robustness than their safety-post-trained counterparts while retaining higher general utility than the teacher: subsequent fine-tuning raises the average attack success rate (ASR) of the 1.7B student by only 5.00%, compared with 11.58% for safety post-training, and its average utility of 48.20% far exceeds the aligned teacher's 27.42%. Unlike conventional large-to-small knowledge distillation, our framework enables selective, small-to-large safety transfer: it reuses the robust safety expertise of a smaller pretrained teacher without inheriting its utility limitations. These findings establish native safety as a reusable model property rather than one permanently tied to the originally pretrained model.

items.title: When LLMs Manipulate: Measuring Behavioral, Social, and Temporal Effects [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.27573v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can influence user trust and decision-making through subtle linguistic cues, yet the behavioral effects of manipulative outputs remain poorly quantified. We introduce a behavioral computing framework for measuring \textit{behavioral vulnerability}, defined as users' susceptibility to manipulative AI responses. Building on DarkPatterns-LLM benchmark, we generate controlled manipulative stimuli using Manipulation Gradient Descent (MGD), targeting biases associated with authority, urgency, and social proof. We analyze participant responses using the Multi-Stakeholder Impact Assessment Network (MSIAN) to model cross-user influence and the Temporal Harm Propagation Model (THPM) to characterize the persistence of behavioral effects over time. In a study involving 120 participants, manipulative framing produced significant changes in trust calibration and compliance ($p < 0.01$), with effects also propagating across social contexts. These findings highlight the need to extend LLM safety evaluation beyond model outputs to measurable behavioral consequences and provide a computational framework for quantifying individual, social, and temporal risks arising from manipulative AI interactions.

items.title: Auditing the Product, Not the Recursion: The Evaluation Evidence Behind Recursive Self-Improvement Claims [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.27610v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) promises AI systems, such as self-evolving LLM agents, that become better at producing further improvements. Evaluating this promise requires separating product claims about the final system from process claims about the improvement process itself. Existing surveys specify the evidence these claims require, but how often studies report that evidence remains unmeasured. We examine this question through full-text coding of 114 eligible studies in a reproducible arXiv search frame frozen in October 2026, including 90 that describe their own systems as RSI. The codebook links claims to evaluation designs. Independent human coding, third-reader adjudication, and a separate blind coding of improver comparisons assess coding reliability. Among the 90 RSI studies, 90% report product evaluation beyond development tasks under a broad criterion that includes partial or unstated separation, while 60% report evaluation on tasks unused for selection. Only 22% audit two or more reruns of the full loop. In a human-coded random sample, the RSI studies show the same contrast: 45% evaluate on tasks unused for selection and 14% audit two or more reruns. Of the 26 studies claiming a better improvement procedure, 23 report a related comparison, but only 4 compare earlier and later procedures from identical starting artifacts at a matched budget. Across these results and a comparison set of established works, evidence for repeatability and improved procedures remains less developed than product evaluation. Three propositions explain how selection effects, shared evaluator errors, and changes in system state limit what product evaluations can establish. Together, the findings support a claim-indexed reporting standard that connects each claim to the evaluation design needed to test it.

items.title: BCT: Bayes-Consistent Tempering for Flow Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.27641v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Temperature scaling is typically applied as a post-hoc transformation of model probabilities. In posterior-induced flow language models, this creates two mismatches. First, posterior tempering implicitly changes both the endpoint distribution and the distribution of intermediate noisy states, while the denoiser remains trained on the original states. Second, the tempered posterior weights are combined with transport dynamics derived for the untempered flow. These mismatches are reflected empirically: lowering temperature improves GSM8K performance much less reliably in flow LMs than in discrete diffusion LMs. We introduce Bayes-Consistent Tempering (BCT), which makes temperature explicit in both the distributions and dynamics of the generative flow. Its learned realization trains the denoiser on tempered intermediate states and tempers the endpoint distribution using the corresponding tempered dynamics. We also derive training-free variants for conventionally trained checkpoints. Across hyperspherical flow LMs with two denoiser architectures and a von Mises--Fisher flow LM, BCT improves GSM8K generation across broad temperature ranges and achieves the strongest tempering performance. The gains also extend to Sudoku, demonstrating benefits on tightly constrained generation. At very low temperatures, the learned realization is also markedly more robust than the training-free variants, supporting temperature as a property of the generative flow across training and inference rather than a post-hoc probability adjustment. Code and model weights are available at https://daioba.github.io/bct .

items.title: CUA-Recovery: Benchmarking Error Recovery in Long-Horizon Computer-Use Agents [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.27645v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As computer-use agents (CUAs) move to long-horizon workflows spanning multiple applications, undetected errors can silently corrupt persistent state and cause cascading failures in subsequent actions. Reliable error detection and recovery have become critical bottlenecks for building robust CUAs. However, existing benchmarks focus primarily on end-to-end task performance, providing limited insight into whether agents can detect and recover from errors during execution. The few benchmarks that evaluate recovery rely largely on manually injected errors, which may not reflect the types or horizons of failures induced by real agent policies. We introduce CUA-Recovery, a benchmark comprising test and training suites across multiple desktop applications. We construct it using ReRail, a framework for synthesizing long-horizon tasks and trajectories in a persistent desktop environment. ReRail composes MyPCBench tasks into new long-horizon workflows with executable ground truth, collects verifier-confirmed failures from multiple policies, and turns them into verified recovery trajectories. CUA-Recovery comprises a human-verified test suite of 2,250 erroneous states over 100 tasks and a training suite of 8.6K trajectories over 377 tasks. Evaluation on the test suite shows that agents struggle both to recognize inherited errors and to complete the task. Across six agents and six takeover depths, Error Awareness Rate (EAR) reaches at most 44.0% and Pass@3 at most 25.5%. After fine-tuning Qwen3.5-35B-A3B on the training suite, its average EAR rises from 19.9% to 35.2% on held-out recovery states, and its Rubric Score goes from 5.0% to 16.1%. It also gains 15.3 points on MyPCBench and 10.8 points on Odysseys for Pass@3, showing that the training trajectories help both with recovery and with completing tasks from a clean start. Our code is available at https://github.com/xu-hu-2002/CUA-Recovery.

items.title: When Does Experience Memory Help Closed-Loop LLM Driving Agents? A Controlled Evaluation with Resampled Warmup Pools, Token-Matched Fillers, and Audited Baselines [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.27714v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: When does experience memory help a closed-loop LLM driving agent? Published gains cannot say, because the two factors we find to matter most, which warmup experiences the pool contains and what any injected tokens do to the prompt, are controlled in none of them. We answer with a controlled evaluation on one audited HighwayEnv testbed (1Hz, gpt-4o-mini for the decisive contrasts). We treat the warmup pool as a resampled random factor (ten disjoint pools) and add token-matched irrelevant-filler controls, oracle-certified diagnostics, caution-pricing metrics, and quantified audits of the baseline ports. The probe suite spans flat-text retrieval (a DiLu port), a single-frame grid port (RESPOND-inspired), our episodic temporal-graph memory, a retrieval-free consolidated rulebook, and a flat K-step observation-history baseline. Four findings follow, each a property of this testbed. (1) Headline memory gains belong to the warmup draw. The reported pool is the best of ten for both retrieval memories, which beat No-Memory in only one pool of ten (sign test p=0.011), and even the rulebook's apparent pool-immunity collapsed on five fresh draws. (2) No retrieval design tested exceeds token-matched filler. The collision-only merge ceiling is reached by a single 15-token caution instruction, and metrics that price caution erase the rulebook's lead. (3) Representational sophistication is nowhere robustly operative. (4) Baseline port quality silently inverts conclusions. On this testbed, a single-pool comparison without filler controls would have reported memory gains that these controls reverse. We release the testbed, audited ports, seeds, and caches.

items.title: Give the Model a Finger: Developmentally Aligned Evaluation of Counting in Vision-Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.27756v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are exact on small sets and drift into estimation on larger ones, a profile reminiscent of children before they master counting. Children cross the barrier with epistemic actions: pointing at each item while reciting number words, moving counted items aside, partitioning the array. We give VLMs the same actions as dumb image tools with no visual intelligence of their own in a training-free agent loop. Our central claim is about measurement, not intervention: a model that counts by marking leaves a normally hidden serial procedure on the image, and the developmental principles of counting turn those marks into an interpretable audit of serial visual reasoning: every tag is classified against point-level ground truth as on-target, duplicate, phantom, or omitted, the answer is checked against the number of tags, and order irrelevance is tested by forcing opposite traversal orders. Across 9 models, 682 images, and 7 harness conditions we find that (i) the exact-counting range is a model-specific signature spanning nearly two orders of magnitude (R80 from 3 to 150 dots); (ii) as an intervention the finger mostly fails: tags help 4 of 9 models on small-count photographs, hurt imprecise pointers, and rarely beat a verbal routine or a blind point list; what the loop buys is an auditable trace, not accuracy; (iii) as measurement it succeeds: a tag-perturbation probe shows that precise pointers read their answers off the tags, pointing precision tracks which models benefit, dense scenes fail by omission, and models rarely revise after seeing their own tags; and (iv) the capacities dissociate: models follow an instructed traversal order yet often change their answer when it reverses, and children's regular-over-scattered advantage appears only under the routine and survives lattices that defeat a rows-times-columns shortcut.

items.title: Lost in Recovery: Demystifying Recovery Behavior of Computer-Use Agents via Goal-Oriented Action Replay [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.27954v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent advances in large (vision) language models have enabled computer-use agents that automate digital workflows via fine-grained keyboard and mouse operations. However, such agents remain fragile in long-horizon settings, where errors accumulate and executed actions leave unintended side effects, making the ability to recover from failures critical. Yet, existing remedies remain inadequate: environment resets are infeasible in proprietary settings, action replay is prohibitively expensive over long horizons, and API-based rollback is limited to web environments, leaving model-based recovery largely unexplored. To address this gap, we present ReTrace, a scalable evaluation framework for systematically studying recovery behavior in computer-use agents. We formalize Transition-Consistent Recovery: identical downstream actions from the recovered and target states must yield identical outcomes. We operationalize this criterion through goal-oriented action replay following controlled error injection. Using ReTrace, we present the first systematic study of autonomous, model-based recovery, revealing that (i) ideal recovery can unlock model's latent task completion capabilities, (ii) current computer-use agents fail to exploit their latent recovery capabilities, and (iii) accurate model-based recovery yields measurable end-to-end gains. Together, these findings establish recovery as a fundamental capability for building reliable computer-use agents. Our code and dataset is available at https://github.com/BangProx/ReTRACE.

items.title: Building Telecom Language Models with RSOD: Domain Data, Specialist Post-Training, Memory-Conscious Distillation, and Networking Evaluation [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.27993v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Telecom language models must combine broad networking knowledge with specialist behavior across routing, broadband services, access technologies, and operational diagnostics while remaining practical to deploy as a single model. We present an end-to-end framework that builds source-grounded synthetic training data from structured networking taxonomies and expert graphs, materializes 212,559 routed training records across fourteen networking routes, trains six frozen specialist LoRA teachers over one shared continued-pretrained backbone, and consolidates their behavior into one deployable student adapter using Routed Specialist On-Policy Distillation (RSOD). In RSOD, the committed student generates each trajectory, the route-assigned specialist teacher-forces the exact native token sequence, compact teacher hidden states are reconstructed through the shared frozen output head, and only the student LoRA is updated. A controlled reconstruction validation shows mean absolute logit error of 7.26 x 10^-6 with 100% top-1 agreement between native and reconstructed teacher logits. On four RTX 6000 Ada GPUs, the completed 2,000-step run produced 16,000 trajectories with zero observed student-version or token- ID mismatches. Under the primary route-conditioned evaluation over 2,850 held-out questions, the raw Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct model scores 12.8661/25 micro (13.0172/25 macro), the combined routed six-teacher system scores 21.7641/25 micro, and the consolidated RSOD student, released as Llama-CalixCLM v1, reaches 21.7112/25 micro (21.8006/25 macro) on the same five dimension LLM-judge rubric. Under a separate neutral deployment-like prompt, the same student reaches 20.0028/25 micro (20.0778/25 macro). The consolidated student remains within 0.0529 micro-score points of the combined routed-teacher system while retaining a numerically validated and auditable train-serve execution path.

items.title: Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-Set Diffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.28543v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Discrete diffusion models iteratively denoise a noisy sequence of categorical data such as text, enabling any-order generation with self-correction and in-filling capabilities. This makes them promising candidates for reasoning, planning, and constrained-generation tasks like coding and math. Yet masked and uniform diffusion erase a token's identity in a single corruption event, so their noisy states cannot explicitly represent partially resolved uncertainty in which several alternatives remain plausible. We close this gap with Binary Discrete Diffusion, a family of continuous-time discrete-diffusion processes whose noisy state is a set of candidate tokens per position, represented as a binary membership vector. Binary diffusion changes candidate sets through additions and removals, allowing information to be lost and recovered gradually while the diffusion state itself represents partial uncertainty. On Sudoku-Extreme, Boxoban, and graph coloring, the symmetric formulation of binary diffusion consistently outperforms strong, well-tuned masked and uniform baselines under matched architectures and controlled training, sampling, and tuning budgets, with its largest gains on the hardest instances, while remaining competitive on language modeling (Text8, TinyStories, OpenWebText). These results support candidate sets as an effective intermediate representation for iterative reasoning and show that the corruption kernel can materially change the computation learned by the reverse model.

items.title: Abstract Compression of Conversational Audio Context for LLM-based ASR [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2603.26246v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Standard LLM-based speech recognition systems process utterances in isolation, limiting their ability to leverage conversational context. Here we study whether multimodal context from prior turns improves LLM-based ASR and how to represent that context efficiently. We find that, after supervised multi-turn training, conversational context mainly helps with the recognition of contextual entities. However, conditioning on raw context is expensive because the prior-turn audio embedding sequence grows rapidly with conversation length. To address this, we propose Abstract Compression, a learned latent abstraction of prior-turn audio that replaces each prior-turn audio sequence with a fixed number of latent tokens while retaining corresponding transcripts explicitly. On both in-domain and out-of-domain test sets, the compression-enabled model recovers part of the gains of raw-context conditioning with a smaller prior-turn audio footprint. We also provide targeted analyses of the compression setup and its tradeoffs.

items.title: Probe, Don't Prompt: A Hidden-State Probe for Metadata Filtering in Multi-Meta-RAG [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2607.03929v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Multi-Meta-RAG improves retrieval for multi-hop question answering by filtering a vector store on metadata, specifically the news source and the publication date, which it extracts from each query using GPT-3.5. This extractor requires a proprietary API call for every query, and its output is not restricted to the allowed sources: even though the prompt specifies 49 sources, GPT-3.5 generates 128 distinct source names, 79 of which do not appear on the list. We show that the source part of this extractor can be replaced by a local, deterministic probe trained on the hidden states of a small open-source language model. The probe is a multi-label logistic classifier on the mean-pooled hidden states of one layer, trained with a class-balanced loss on the gold evidence sources. Using 5-fold cross-validation to select the layer, we evaluate four models ranging from 135M to 1.5B parameters out-of-fold across all 2556 MultiHop-RAG queries. The probe reaches a set-exact accuracy of 90.9%, compared to 88.0% for a substring baseline and 80.9% for GPT-3.5. The difference comes from null queries, for which GPT-3.5 never predicts an empty source set. Across the remaining queries, all three methods achieve set-exact accuracies within 1.1 percentage points of each other. Unlike earlier probing work, we use the probe as a component of a retrieval pipeline rather than for interpretation. For all four models, the cross-validation selects one of the first layers, in contrast to the middle layers reported for retrieval tasks. We attribute this to the source name appearing verbatim in 95.4% of gold query-source pairs. The 135M model is 1.5 percentage points less accurate than the 1.5B model, so the filter requires only a partial forward pass through a small model and one linear layer. The code is available at https://github.com/mxpoliakov/Multi-Meta-RAG.

items.title: Knowledge That Is Linear Before Fine-Tuning Generalizes After It [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.22300v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Not all facts a language model can recall support further learning equally well. We distinguish active facts, which support generalization beyond their own recall, from inert facts, which can be recalled but do not support such generalization in a given task. We study this distinction by constructing new relations from existing ones. Take the relation that maps a place to its continent (Paris -> Europe) and assign each of its answers an arbitrary new label (Europe -> crab, Asia -> zebra). The new relation then maps Paris -> crab. We fine-tune the model on the new relation for a subset of subjects, without telling it the original relation or the relabeling rule, and test whether it assigns the corresponding labels to held-out subjects that share an answer in the original relation. Having learned Paris -> crab, does it answer Munich -> crab? Across eleven language models and 70 relations, how linearly readable the original relation is in pretrained representations strongly predicts this generalization. Within each model, the two correlate across relations at Pearson r = 0.87 to 0.92. This association persists when controlling, separately and jointly, for the number of fine-tuning subjects and answers, the model's accuracy on the original relation, and how often the subjects occur in pretraining text. It is also robust to re-randomizing the label assignment and fine-tuning seed, and to replacing the animal labels with labels from thirteen other semantic categories. When we map a fine-tuned model's wrong label back to the original answer it was assigned to, Munich -> zebra becomes Munich -> Asia. Answers recovered this way are more often among the linear probe's top answers for the subject than among the pretrained model's own. Whether a new relation generalizes depends less on whether its facts can be recalled than on how readily their shared structure can be read out linearly.

items.title: TTCS: Test-Time Curriculum Synthesis for Self-Evolving [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2601.22628v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Test-Time Training offers a promising way to improve the reasoning ability of large language models (LLMs) by adapting the model using only the test questions. However, existing methods struggle with difficult reasoning problems for two reasons: raw test questions are often too difficult to yield high-quality pseudo-labels, and the limited size of test sets makes continuous online updates prone to instability. To address these limitations, we propose TTCS, a co-evolving test-time training framework. Specifically, TTCS initializes two policies from the same pretrained model: a question synthesizer and a reasoning solver. These policies evolve through iterative optimization: the synthesizer generates progressively challenging question variants conditioned on the test questions, creating a structured curriculum tailored to the solver's current capability, while the solver updates itself using self-consistency rewards computed from multiple sampled responses on both original test and synthetic questions. Crucially, the solver's feedback guides the synthesizer to generate questions aligned with the model's current capability, and the generated question variants in turn stabilize the solver's test-time training. Experiments show that TTCS consistently strengthens the reasoning ability on challenging mathematical benchmarks and transfers to general-domain tasks across different LLM backbones, highlighting a scalable path towards dynamically constructing test-time curricula for self-evolving. Our code and implementation details are available at https://github.com/XMUDeepLIT/TTCS.
